reviewer: Codex individual static inspection; no independent human review yet
scope: Reviewed sites and interfaces only; no module-wide proof of absence of obfuscation; no malicious behavior executed

findings: func[48] has 141 br_table instructions. At 0xf8bc and 0xf97e, dispatch selectors are signed bytes loaded from constant addresses 11266 and 11274. Arithmetic branches update local 2 using multiplication or addition and converge via br. This is data-directed arithmetic dispatch, not merely a high branch count.
func[55] tests byte value 37 (%), advances a pointer, and dispatches on signed character values minus 37 or 65. Character/format parsing is a plausible explanation for its large tables.
Exports k/l/m/n and missing name section show opaque naming but do not identify an obfuscator or intent.
reviews.alternative_explanations: Data-directed arithmetic may implement the mining algorithm itself or an interpreter; format parsing can explain library branch tables. No matching original or transformation history has yet established obfuscation.
reviews.follow_up: Inspect the data-directed arithmetic routine and compare a documented source implementation before claiming virtualization or control-flow flattening.

findings: func[37] reinterprets f64 bits as i64, shifts right by 52 and masks with 2047 before br_table at 0x90fb. The selector is the floating-point exponent field.
That table has 2049 label entries, but only three distinct depths: 2047 entries are depth 2, one is depth 0 and one depth 1. Table length is not the number of distinct control destinations.
func[64] dispatches on bytes after testing % and on signed character values minus 65/91. These sites support a character-parser explanation rather than evidence of a central obfuscation dispatcher.
reviews.alternative_explanations: Floating-point special-case handling and format parsing explain the reviewed sites. No conclusion about every other function is made.

findings: Reviewed loop dispatch sign-extends an 8-bit value; another table uses a selector minus ASCII 65. The surrounding code updates a pointer and stores through memory. Character parsing is an alternative to flattening.

Export prefix _JtsgOXcVkUs_ is opaque. The entire code-section payload exactly equals that of 65debcbe8c6e64a04c9c3b75794b77644526a514d89a09f037f2cf53f2aa2f98, whose corresponding export prefix is _bBcDYnZGHoa_. Data sections also differ.
The matching code payload SHA-256 is a3b1e6387953b49c5538f2cb0471fc68ab982cc3165130590aefc59180d91e7c. This establishes code identity, not common malware family or a known parent.
reviews.alternative_explanations: Naming may be identifier substitution or a build-specific naming scheme; intention and generator are unverified. Different whole-file hashes overstate code diversity in this pair.

findings: Individually inspected the same three character-dependent branch sites as in c1be4071ccc59e468803cb9b9eae25ec3aaff24f1d37ee0b81ba9126f8334572. Code-section bytes match exactly, despite different module hashes.

Exports use _bBcDYnZGHoa_create/destroy/hash where the paired module uses _JtsgOXcVkUs_create/destroy/hash. Both lack name sections. Data payload hashes differ; this is not claimed to be an exports-only change.
reviews.alternative_explanations: Opaque export naming is confirmed as a property; malicious obfuscation intent and shared generation origin remain unproven.

findings: Getters return low/high parts of globals 11..15; reset function sets those five globals to zero. Counter update sequences global.get N; i64.const 1; i64.add; global.set N occur throughout the code.

Observed exact four-instruction update sequences: global 11:1573, 12:302, 13:1077, 14:523, 15:576. Total 4051 sequences / 16204 instructions, out of 47033 decoded static instructions. This is a static code-composition count, not execution frequency or measured runtime overhead.

The same module is present at SEISMIC CoinHive/64-bit/cryptonight_obfuscated.wasm. The pinned inline_counter64.py explicitly inserts increments for globals 11..15 for add/and/shl/shr_u/xor, consistent with the observed code.

The two reviewed br_table sites use rotated arithmetic selectors and forward blocks, with no enclosing loop. The export prefix thginotpyrc is cryptonight reversed, an identifier-hiding candidate; counter presence does not prove that the module has no other obfuscation.
reviews.alternative_explanations: Instrumentation is an evidenced explanation for much of the added instruction count. Neither this file's malicious deployment nor the complete transformation chain is independently established.

findings: func[31] adds -224 to parameter 0 and combines right-shift 5 with left-shift 27 before forward branch tables. Cases return an error code or initialize/copy memory. These two tables are not enclosed by a loop.
Meaningful exports include _setJob, _mLoop, _mResult and _fromHex. High data entropy 7.918 and absence of a name section do not establish encrypted strings or control-flow flattening.
reviews.alternative_explanations: Ordinary case selection and cryptographic constants remain plausible. No module-wide absence claim.

findings: The inspected tables use the parameter-derived add -224 / shifts 5 and 27 selector, then forward blocks and memory initialization. No loop encloses these sites.

Exports include _dryptonight_create/destroy/hash, a near-name variant of cryptonight. The naming is a candidate concealment feature; the binary alone does not prove deliberate renaming or identify a transformer.
reviews.alternative_explanations: Ordinary build naming and cryptographic switch logic have not been excluded.

findings: Rechecked the two branch-table sites after this previously purposeful case was independently selected by the fixed random seed. Both lie outside loops and use memory-derived selectors.
Name information and _cryptonight_hash_variant_0/1/2 exports remain. The high-entropy data and branch tables alone do not establish a specific obfuscation technique.
reviews.alternative_explanations: Algorithmic case selection and cryptographic tables are plausible; preserve the earlier review.md for fuller evidence.

findings: The reviewed function 29 reads successive signed bytes and tests ASCII 37 (%), then dispatches on character values. This supports a parsing explanation for these branch tables.

Compared all 59 function bodies with independently sampled 4ab6ed5e: 57 are byte-identical; data payloads match. In function 40 this module applies i64.xor 0 and i64.sub 0 to a shift-count value. Both operations are algebraic identities. Function 71 differs too; saved unified differences provide the exact instructions.
Opaque export prefix _XOuJTMJpKnE_ is a naming candidate. Exact whole-file nonmatching to reference seeds does not establish an individual generation parent.
reviews.alternative_explanations: Neutral operations are confirmed locally. The specific generator, intention, and parent of this file are unverified; paired modules are not asserted to be behaviorally identical.

findings: Function 32 dispatches on (memory value >> 8) & 3; function 33 dispatches on a rotated arithmetic selector and copies memory in forward cases. Neither table is inside a loop.
Meaningful _cryptonight_create/destroy/hash exports remain. Data entropy 7.909 matches other inspected mining-related cases, but this does not demonstrate encrypted strings.
reviews.alternative_explanations: Algorithmic case dispatch and cryptographic tables remain plausible. No module-wide absence or malware deployment claim.

findings: Individually inspected function 29 character-based dispatch, including a pointer advance, signed-byte load and test against ASCII 37.

Function 40 lacks the xor-zero/subtract-zero sequence present in the paired file. Pairwise differences are saved; neither file is designated as the original.

findings: Function 38 selects calls to _genstep1 through _genstep9 using parameter 0 minus 1. The branches exit forward and do not form a central looping dispatcher.
Exports retain _mine and data contains a JavaScript submit/Pointer_stringify string. These are clues to host interaction, not proof that JavaScript was moved into Wasm for concealment.

Comparison with 1d38d08e shows 53/54 identical function bodies and identical data payloads. Only function 39 differs at the body-byte level; additional non-code differences account for the larger whole-file size.
reviews.alternative_explanations: The paired difference does not establish which version is original or a shared generation parent. Full loader behavior and maliciousness remain unverified.

findings: Function 38 performs the same forward _genstep1..9 case dispatch as 2eb0e7c2.
In function 39, before a call to _sha256_transf, local 3 is passed through i32.const 0; i32.sub; i32.const 0; i32.shr_u. This preserves its value and is locally redundant arithmetic.
The pair has 53/54 identical function bodies and equal data payloads. Differences are preserved in pair-comparisons/2eb0e7c2-1d38d08e.diff.txt.

findings: Inspected the complete single-function disassembly: constant 16, constant 0, subtraction, constant 0, unsigned right shift, end. The function deterministically leaves 16; both arithmetic operations are neutral.

The module exports memory and data, imports nothing, and contains readable HTML for a popup/banner. It is primarily a data carrier with a small accessor, not evidence of a substantial hidden mining algorithm.
A companion JavaScript consumer was not inspected. Wasm-as-container and JavaScript-to-Wasm logic migration cannot be equated. The author malware label is kept separate from observed content.
reviews.alternative_explanations: The neutral getter can result from mutation. Readable HTML and a popup are insufficient to independently establish malicious deployment or a specific obfuscation strategy.

findings: Exports are short identifiers such as R/S/T, while readable data includes decodeVideoBuffer, audioBuffer and videoBuffer. Name stripping or minification is a candidate property in this author-benign module.
Inspected two tables and their surrounding memory loads, pointer advances and calls. Neither inspected excerpt establishes a control-flow flattening transformation.
This benign-labeled case has high data entropy (7.212), 81 branch tables and 21 inside loops. Those markers alone are not evidence of malware obfuscation.
reviews.alternative_explanations: Media processing, parser/library logic and size-oriented symbol minification can explain the observations. Actual functionality and independent benignness were not dynamically verified.

findings: Exports parse/with_default_config and wasm-bindgen allocation helpers, along with readable Rust runtime and parser error strings, support a parser/library interpretation.

Functions 10 and 11 use range-checked character-derived selectors, then advance pointers and compare loaded bytes to newline (10). This is consistent with parsing rather than a demonstrated obfuscation dispatcher.
Data entropy is 7.452 despite numerous readable error messages. A high-entropy section is not equivalent to encrypted strings.
reviews.alternative_explanations: Language runtime, lookup data and parsing logic are plausible explanations; no module-wide absence claim.

findings: The inspected routine dispatches on sign-extended bytes and characters minus 65; data includes printf-like r=%i, s=%i and formatting literals.
Redundant structures occur in this author-benign file: subtraction of zero before a branch table, nop at 0x7c8c, and instructions after unconditional branches that are unreachable along that path.
The large number of locals and explicit control blocks are observable properties. They do not by themselves identify an obfuscator.
reviews.alternative_explanations: Unoptimized or transformed compiler output and library code are plausible. Redundant-code markers cannot be used as a malware-specific indicator.

findings: Inspected checksum-comparison wrappers calling memcmp, a time wrapper dividing env.current_time by 1000000, and an authorization wrapper calling env.require_auth2.
Exports and data refer to eosio, permission_level and apply. This is evidence for a smart-contract-oriented environment, which must not automatically be grouped with browser-deployed programs.
These small wrappers have direct operations and calls; the reviewed sites provide no positive evidence of a named obfuscation technique.
reviews.alternative_explanations: Only the listed wrapper functions were inspected. The full contract and the author benign label have not been independently validated.

findings: The module imports memory and has no data section. Lack of embedded strings is therefore not evidence that strings were encrypted.
Function 36 loads successive signed bytes, updates a pointer and uses character-dependent branch tables, including a selector minus 65. This resembles the parsing routines in other inspected modules.
The meaningful _hash_cn export remains. External memory initialization and companion JavaScript were not inspected.
reviews.alternative_explanations: Data may be supplied by the host; the module alone cannot establish hiding or absence of strings in the application.

findings: Inspected the complete function exported as sad. It loads pairs of bytes, subtracts them, derives a sign mask with arithmetic right shift 31, and computes (difference XOR sign) - sign before accumulating. Byte differences are within -255..255, so this is absolute difference without overflow ambiguity.
The first loop performs four repeated byte comparisons per iteration; a second loop handles the remainder. This is consistent with loop unrolling and sum-of-absolute-differences computation.
The absence of data/name sections and the xor/shift operations do not establish obfuscation.
reviews.alternative_explanations: Ordinary arithmetic optimization explains the reviewed function; no independent verification of deployment or author benignness.
